topics.name: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
topics.summary: This topic covers the International System of Units (SI): the 7 fundamental (base) units \(-\) metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela \(-\) plus the 2 supplementary units, radian and steradian, which measure plane and solid angle and are themselves dimensionless. Every other physical quantity is measured in a derived unit built from these base units by multiplication and division, such as the newton (kg\(\cdot\)m\(\cdot\)s\(^{-2}\)) for force or the pascal (N/m\(^2\)) for pressure. A large part of working with units is converting cleanly between scales \(-\) SI prefixes such as kilo, centi, and milli, or between SI and CGS systems \(-\) by multiplying or dividing by the correct power of ten for each dimension involved. Getting the number of powers of ten right, especially for units that involve area or volume (which need the conversion factor applied twice or three times), is the main source of error here, alongside keeping track of which quantities are fundamental and which are derived.
key_formulas: \(1\text{ m}^3=10^6\text{ cm}^3\) (apply the length conversion factor three times for volume)
topics.worked_example:
Convert a density of \(2.5\text{ g/cm}^3\) to SI units (kg/m\(^3\)).

\(1\text{ g/cm}^3 = \dfrac{10^{-3}\text{ kg}}{10^{-6}\text{ m}^3}=10^3\text{ kg/m}^3\), so \(2.5\text{ g/cm}^3=2.5\times10^3\text{ kg/m}^3\).
common_mistakes: Treating a derived unit (like the newton or pascal) as if it were a fundamental unit.
Forgetting that the supplementary units radian and steradian are themselves dimensionless, \([M^0L^0T^0]\).
Applying a length conversion factor only once when converting an area or volume, instead of squaring or cubing it.
Losing track of powers of ten when chaining multiple unit conversions in one problem.

topics.name: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
topics.summary: This topic covers how length, mass, and time are actually measured in the lab using common instruments \(-\) metre scales, vernier calipers, screw gauges, and stopwatches or beam balances \(-\) and the central idea of least count: the smallest change in a quantity an instrument can reliably resolve. For a vernier caliper, the least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division; for a screw gauge, it is the pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular scale. Real instruments often carry a zero error \(-\) a constant offset when the jaws are closed or the screw is at zero \(-\) which must be subtracted (if positive) or added back (if negative) to every raw reading to get the true value. Taking several readings and averaging, or timing many repetitions of a periodic event together (like 20 oscillations of a pendulum) rather than just one, are standard techniques for reducing the effect of a coarse least count on the final result.
key_formulas: Screw gauge least count: \(\text{LC}=\dfrac{\text{Pitch}}{\text{Number of circular scale divisions}}\)
Reading \(=\text{MSR}+(\text{CSR}\times\text{LC})\), then corrected for zero error
Corrected reading \(=\) Observed reading \(-\) Zero error
topics.worked_example:
A screw gauge (pitch \(1\) mm, \(100\) divisions, zero error \(+0.003\) cm) reads MSR \(=0.4\) cm and CSR \(=22\).

Least count \(=1/100=0.01\) mm \(=0.001\) cm; observed reading \(=0.4+(22\times0.001)=0.422\) cm; corrected reading \(=0.422-0.003=0.419\) cm.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to correct for a nonzero zero error, or applying its sign backwards.
Mixing up the least-count formulas for a vernier caliper and a screw gauge.
Not converting the least count into the same unit as the main scale reading before adding.
Timing only a single oscillation instead of several, which needlessly inflates the effective timing uncertainty.

topics.name: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
topics.summary: This topic distinguishes accuracy (how close a measurement is to the true value) from precision (how close repeated measurements are to each other), and covers how to quantify the error in a set of readings using mean value, absolute error, mean absolute error, and percentage error. The most important \(-\) and most commonly mistested \(-\) skill is combining the errors of two separately measured quantities when they are combined mathematically: for a sum or difference, the absolute errors always add; for a product or quotient, the fractional (percentage) errors always add; and for a quantity raised to a power \(n\), the fractional error is multiplied by \(n\). In every one of these rules, errors add \(-\) they are never subtracted, even when the quantities themselves are being subtracted or divided, because an error represents an uncertainty in either direction, and uncertainties cannot cancel.
key_formulas: Sum or difference: \(\Delta Z=\Delta A+\Delta B\)
Product or quotient: \(\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z}=\dfrac{\Delta A}{A}+\dfrac{\Delta B}{B}\)
topics.worked_example:
\(A=(4.0\pm0.1)\) and \(B=(2.0\pm0.1)\); find the percentage error in \(Z=A/B\).

\(\%\text{ error in }A=\dfrac{0.1}{4.0}\times100=2.5\%\); \(\%\text{ error in }B=\dfrac{0.1}{2.0}\times100=5\%\); since \(Z\) is a quotient, these add: total \(\%\text{ error}=2.5\%+5\%=7.5\%\), even though \(Z\) itself is a division.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the fractional errors for a quotient or difference instead of always adding them.
Forgetting to divide the sum of absolute deviations by the number of readings when finding the mean absolute error.
Confusing a precise-but-inaccurate result with an accurate one, or vice versa.
Forgetting to multiply the fractional error by the exponent \(n\) for a quantity raised to a power.

topics.name: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
topics.summary: This topic covers the rules for counting significant figures in a measured number and for carrying that precision correctly through arithmetic. All nonzero digits are significant, as are zeros between nonzero digits; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant, but trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous and best written in scientific notation to make the intended precision clear. The critical rule, and the central trap in this topic, is that addition and subtraction limit the result by the fewest number of decimal places among the terms, while multiplication and division limit the result by the fewest number of significant figures among the terms \(-\) these are two different rules, and applying the wrong one to a given operation is the single most common error. Rounding follows the simple round-half-up convention: a digit of 5 or more rounds the preceding digit up.
key_formulas: Addition/subtraction: result's decimal places \(=\) fewest decimal places among the terms
Multiplication/division: result's significant figures \(=\) fewest significant figures among the terms
Example: \(12.3+5.62=17.9\) (1 decimal place, not 3 significant figures)
Example: \(4.5\times2.10=9.5\) (2 significant figures, not 1 decimal place)
topics.worked_example:
Add \(12.36\) and \(4.1\).

\(12.36+4.1=16.46\), but \(4.1\) has only 1 decimal place, so the sum is rounded to 1 decimal place: \(16.5\).
common_mistakes: Applying the multiplication/division significant-figure rule to an addition or subtraction problem, or vice versa.
Miscounting significant figures in numbers with zeros, especially ambiguous trailing zeros in whole numbers.
Using banker's rounding (round-half-to-even) instead of the simple round-half-up convention.
Adding an extra digit to a final answer that the least-precise input does not actually justify.

topics.name: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
topics.summary: This topic uses the dimensional formula of a quantity \(-\) its dependence on mass, length, and time written as \([M^aL^bT^c]\) \(-\) to check whether an equation is dimensionally consistent, to convert a quantity's value from one unit system to another, and to derive how one quantity depends on others up to an unknown dimensionless constant. Dimensionless quantities, such as angle, strain, or refractive index, still have a dimensional formula \(-\) it is simply \([M^0L^0T^0]\), never \`\`no formula.'' Two critical limits define what dimensional analysis can and cannot do: it can never determine a dimensionless numerical constant appearing in a formula (such as \(\tfrac12\) or \(2\pi\)), and dimensional consistency is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for an equation to be correct \(-\) a dimensionally consistent equation can still be numerically wrong.
topics.worked_example:
Check whether \(v=u+at\) is dimensionally consistent.

Each term has dimensional formula \([M^0L^1T^{-1}]\) (velocity, and acceleration \(\times\) time), so the equation is dimensionally consistent \(-\) though this alone cannot confirm any numerical coefficient in the formula is correct.
common_mistakes: Claiming a dimensionless quantity has no dimensional formula, or inventing a nonzero one for it.
Believing dimensional analysis can determine a dimensionless numerical constant like \(\tfrac12\) or \(2\pi\).
Treating dimensional consistency as proof that an equation is numerically correct.
Mixing up the dimensional formulae of similar-looking quantities, such as work and torque, which share \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\) despite being physically different.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the seven SI base units?
questions.explanation:
The seven SI base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela.

Kilogram is the base unit for mass, so it is correct.

Newton, joule, and watt are all derived units expressed in terms of the base units, not base units themselves.
questions.hint: Ask which option names a quantity, not a combination of quantities.
distractor_logic: Newton is a derived unit built from kg, m and s (force = mass \(\times\) acceleration); it is not one of the seven base units.
Joule is a derived unit (kg\(\cdot\)m\(^2\cdot\)s\(^{-2}\)); frequent everyday use makes it feel basic, but it is built from the base units.
Watt is a derived unit for power (energy per time); it is not among the seven fundamental SI units.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: What are the SI units for plane angle and solid angle respectively?
questions.explanation:
Plane angle and solid angle are measured using two supplementary SI units, in addition to the seven base units.

Radian is the SI unit of plane angle, and steradian is the SI unit of solid angle.
questions.hint: One of these two units applies to a flat angle and the other to a 3-D angular spread.
distractor_logic: Degree is not an SI unit at all; only radian is the accepted SI unit for plane angle.
This ignores that solid angle has its own distinct SI unit, steradian, and wrongly reuses radian for both.
The two units are swapped; radian belongs to plane angle and steradian belongs to solid angle.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert 5 kilometres into metres.
questions.explanation:
The prefix kilo- means a multiplying factor of \(10^3\).

So \(5\text{ km} = 5\times10^3\text{ m} = 5000\text{ m}\).
questions.hint: Kilo- always multiplies the base unit by a thousand.
distractor_logic: Dividing by 100 instead of multiplying by 1000, as if the kilo- prefix meant a factor of \(10^{-2}\).
Using a factor of 100 for the kilo- prefix instead of the correct factor of 1000.
Inverting the conversion direction, treating kilometres as smaller than metres instead of larger.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The SI base unit of electric current is:
questions.explanation:
Ampere is one of the seven SI base units and is used to measure electric current.

Coulomb, volt, and ohm are all derived from ampere combined with other base units.
questions.hint: This unit is named after a famous 19th-century physicist who studied electrodynamics.
distractor_logic: Coulomb is the derived unit of electric charge (ampere \(\times\) second), not the base unit of current.
Volt is the derived unit of electric potential difference, not of current.
Ohm is the derived unit of electrical resistance, not of current.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Which of these is a derived SI unit rather than one of the seven base units?
questions.explanation:
Pascal is defined as newton per square metre (\(\text{N/m}^2\)), which itself expands into kg, m, and s — so pascal is a derived unit.

Kelvin, mole, and candela are each independent base units.
questions.hint: Three of the four options are base units; only one combines other units together.
distractor_logic: Kelvin is one of the seven SI base units, used directly for thermodynamic temperature.
Mole is one of the seven SI base units, not a combination of other units.
Candela is one of the seven SI base units, not built from other base units.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Express 250 milligrams in kilograms.
questions.hint: Milligram to kilogram needs two prefix steps, not one.
distractor_logic: Converting mg to g correctly but then mislabeling the resulting number as kilograms without the second \(10^{-3}\) step.
Applying only one factor of \(10^{-3}\) and then miscounting the remaining powers of ten.
Treating milli-to-kilo as a single \(10^{-3}\) step instead of the combined \(10^{-6}\) needed for mg to kg.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The mole is the SI base unit used to measure:
questions.explanation:
The mole is the SI base unit for the physical quantity called amount of substance, counted in terms of a fixed number of elementary entities.

Mass, molar concentration, and number density are related but distinct quantities with their own units.
questions.hint: This is the base quantity, not any of the several related chemistry quantities built from it.
distractor_logic: Mass is measured in kilograms; mole counts entities (like atoms or molecules), not mass directly.
Molar concentration (mol/L) is a derived quantity built from mole and volume, not the base quantity itself.
Number density (particles per volume) is a derived quantity combining a count with volume; mole alone measures amount of substance.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert 2 hours into seconds.
questions.explanation:
1 hour \(= 60\) minutes \(= 3600\) seconds.

So \(2\text{ h} = 2\times3600\text{ s} = 7200\text{ s}\).
questions.hint: There are two multiplication steps: hours to minutes, then minutes to seconds.
distractor_logic: Converting hours to minutes correctly (2 h = 120 min) but forgetting the further minutes-to-seconds step.
Computing the number of seconds in 1 hour instead of 2 hours.
Using 36000 seconds per hour instead of the correct 3600 seconds per hour, an extra factor of 10.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: What is the general formula for the least count of a vernier caliper?
options: value of the smallest main-scale division divided by the total number of divisions on the vernier scale
value of the smallest main-scale division multiplied by the number of divisions on the vernier scale
value of the smallest main-scale division divided by the number of main-scale divisions
sum of the smallest main-scale and vernier-scale divisions
questions.explanation:
The least count of a vernier caliper equals the value of one main-scale division divided by the total number of divisions on the vernier scale.

Equivalently, it is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division (1 MSD \(-\) 1 VSD).
questions.hint: Least count tells you the smallest length the instrument can resolve beyond the main scale.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relationship, turning a division into a multiplication.
Uses the wrong scale's division count (main scale) instead of the vernier scale's division count.
Adds the two division values instead of dividing the main-scale division by the vernier division count.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A vernier caliper's main scale has divisions of 1 mm, and 10 vernier divisions coincide with 9 main-scale divisions. What is its least count?
questions.hint: First find the value of one vernier division, then subtract it from one main-scale division.
distractor_logic: Off by one decimal place, from forgetting to convert the result from millimetres to centimetres.
Reports the vernier-scale division value itself rather than the least count difference.
Reports the main-scale division value directly instead of computing the least count.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: For a screw gauge with pitch 1 mm and 100 divisions on the circular (head) scale, the least count is:
questions.explanation:
Least count of a screw gauge \(=\dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{number of circular-scale divisions}}\).

\(=\dfrac{1\text{ mm}}{100} = 0.01\) mm.
questions.hint: Pitch is the distance moved per full rotation; least count is a fraction of that.
distractor_logic: Divides the pitch by 10 instead of 100, off by one decimal place.
Multiplies the pitch by the number of divisions instead of dividing by it.
Uses the pitch value itself as the least count, ignoring the circular-scale divisions.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: The pitch of a screw gauge is defined as:
options: the distance between two consecutive divisions on the circular scale
the least count of the instrument
the total length of the main scale
the linear distance moved by the screw for one complete rotation of the circular scale
questions.explanation:
Pitch is how far the screw advances linearly along the main scale for one full rotation of the circular scale.

Dividing the pitch by the number of divisions on the circular scale gives the least count, so the two are not the same quantity.
questions.hint: Think of pitch as the linear advance per full turn of the thimble.
distractor_logic: Confuses pitch, a linear-scale property, with the angular spacing of head-scale divisions.
Pitch and least count are related but distinct; pitch divided by the number of head divisions gives least count.
Confuses pitch, a small per-rotation distance, with the overall length of the linear scale.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: Which instrument is best suited for accurately measuring the diameter of a thin wire (a fraction of a millimetre)?
questions.explanation:
A screw gauge typically has a least count of about 0.01 mm, ten times finer than a vernier caliper's typical 0.1 mm.

This makes it the right choice for measuring small diameters like that of a thin wire.
questions.hint: Compare typical least counts: metre scale > vernier caliper > screw gauge in coarseness.
distractor_logic: A metre scale's smallest division (about 1 mm) is far too coarse to resolve sub-millimetre wire diameters.
Its least count (typically 0.01 cm, i.e. 0.1 mm) is coarser than a screw gauge's 0.01 mm, so it is less precise for very thin wires.
Designed for large lengths with coarse divisions, unsuitable for sub-millimetre precision.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A positive zero error in a vernier caliper means:
options: the zero of the vernier scale lies to the left of the main scale zero when the jaws are closed
the zero of the vernier scale lies to the right of the zero of the main scale when the jaws are fully closed
the instrument reads exactly zero when the jaws are closed
the measured reading is smaller than the true value
questions.explanation:
With a positive zero error, the vernier zero is displaced to the right of the main-scale zero when the jaws touch.

This causes every reading to be larger than the true value, so the zero error must be subtracted from raw readings.
questions.hint: Right-shifted vernier zero means the instrument over-reads.
distractor_logic: This describes a negative zero error, not a positive one.
This describes the absence of any zero error, not a positive error.
A positive zero error makes the instrument read larger than the true value, not smaller.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: To reduce timing error while measuring the time period of a simple pendulum with a stopwatch, a student should:
options: measure the time for a single oscillation using the same stopwatch
time one oscillation but repeat the process 20 times and add the results
measure the total time for a large number of oscillations (say 20) and divide by that number
use a longer pendulum instead of timing multiple oscillations
questions.explanation:
A stopwatch's reaction-time error is roughly fixed in absolute size no matter how long the measured interval is.

Timing many oscillations together makes that fixed error a much smaller fraction of the total time, and dividing by the count then gives a more accurate period.
questions.hint: A fixed timing error matters less when spread over a longer measured interval.
distractor_logic: A single oscillation is too short, so the fixed reaction-time error becomes a large fraction of the measured value.
Adding repeated single-oscillation timings does not average out the reaction-time error the way timing many oscillations at once does.
Changing the pendulum's length changes the period itself but does not address the reaction-time error in starting and stopping the stopwatch.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A beam balance is primarily used to measure:
options: weight, by direct reading of a spring's extension
mass, by comparing an object against known standard masses
questions.explanation:
A beam balance compares the unknown mass on one pan against known standard masses on the other pan until the beam balances.

It therefore measures mass, not weight, length, or time.
questions.hint: Beam balances work by comparison, not by reading a scale directly.
distractor_logic: This describes a spring balance, which measures weight (a force), not a beam balance.
Length is measured with rulers, vernier calipers, or screw gauges, not a beam balance.
This function is unrelated to what a beam balance does.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Accuracy of a measurement refers to:
options: how close the measured value is to the true value
how close repeated measurements are to one another
the number of decimal places reported in a measurement
the least count of the measuring instrument
questions.explanation:
Accuracy describes how close a measured value comes to the actual, true value of the quantity.

It is a distinct idea from precision, which is about the spread among repeated readings.
questions.hint: Accuracy is about correctness relative to the true value.
distractor_logic: This describes precision, not accuracy.
Decimal places relate to the instrument's resolution and significant figures, not to closeness to the true value.
Least count is a property of the instrument's resolution, not a statement about closeness to the true value.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Precision of a measurement refers to:
options: how close a measurement is to the true value
how close repeated measurements of the same quantity are to one another
the absolute error of a single measurement
the total number of significant figures in a reading
questions.explanation:
Precision reflects how tightly clustered repeated readings of the same quantity are, regardless of whether they are near the true value.

A set of readings can be precise (tightly clustered) yet inaccurate (clustered away from the true value).
questions.hint: Precision is about consistency among repeated trials, not correctness.
distractor_logic: This describes accuracy, not precision.
Absolute error is defined relative to the true or mean value, not the closeness of readings to each other.
Significant figures indicate the reported resolution of a single number, not how tightly repeated readings cluster.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: The absolute error of a measurement is defined as:
options: the ratio of the error to the true value
the error expressed as a percentage
the magnitude of the difference between the measured value and the true (or mean) value
the sum of all individual measurement errors
questions.explanation:
Absolute error is simply \(|\text{measured value} - \text{true (or mean) value}|\), carrying the same units as the quantity itself.

Relative and percentage error build further on this basic definition.
questions.hint: Absolute error keeps the same units as the original measurement.
distractor_logic: This defines relative error, not absolute error.
This defines percentage error, which is relative error multiplied by 100.
This describes a total across many readings, not the error of a single measurement relative to the true or mean value.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Five readings of a length are 19.8 cm, 20.2 cm, 19.9 cm, 20.1 cm, and 20.0 cm, with mean 20.0 cm. The mean absolute error is:
questions.explanation:
The deviations from the mean are 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1, and 0.0 cm.

Their sum is 0.6 cm, and dividing by the 5 readings gives a mean absolute error of \(0.6/5 = 0.12\) cm.
questions.hint: Average the magnitudes of the individual deviations from the mean, don't just add them.
distractor_logic: Reports the sum of the absolute deviations directly, without dividing by the number of readings.
Takes the single largest individual deviation as if it were the mean absolute error, instead of averaging all five deviations.
Divides the sum of deviations by 25 (mistakenly squaring the count of readings) instead of by 5.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Relative error of a measurement is defined as:
options: the absolute error divided by the true (or mean) value
the true value divided by the absolute error
the absolute error divided by the number of readings
questions.explanation:
Relative error \(=\dfrac{\text{absolute error}}{\text{true (or mean) value}}\).

Because it is a ratio of two quantities with the same units, relative error itself is dimensionless.
questions.hint: Relative error is a ratio, so it carries no units.
distractor_logic: This step alone gives percentage error's numerator relationship only after already dividing by the true value; multiplying the raw absolute error by 100 skips that division.
This inverts the correct ratio.
Confuses relative error, a ratio to the true value, with an unrelated per-reading average.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Percentage error of a measurement is calculated as:
options: mean absolute error minus relative error
questions.explanation:
Percentage error \(=\) relative error \(\times 100\%\), i.e. \(\dfrac{\text{absolute error}}{\text{true value}}\times100\).

It expresses the relative error as a percentage for easier interpretation.
questions.hint: Percentage error builds directly on relative error by scaling it to a percentage.
distractor_logic: Skips dividing by the true or mean value first, so the result does not correctly express a percentage of the true value.
Inverts the required operation; percentage error needs multiplication by 100, not division.
This subtraction has no physical meaning; percentage error is not formed by subtracting these two quantities.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A measurement is described as precise but not accurate when:
options: repeated readings are scattered widely but average close to the true value
a single reading exactly matches the true value
repeated readings cluster tightly together but consistently lie away from the true value
the instrument has a very coarse least count
questions.explanation:
Precision concerns how tightly repeated readings cluster together, independent of where that cluster sits relative to the true value.

If the cluster is tight but offset from the true value, the readings are precise without being accurate — often a sign of a systematic error.
questions.hint: Picture a target: precise-but-inaccurate shots land close together but off-centre.
distractor_logic: This describes readings that are closer to accurate on average, but not precise, since they are not tightly clustered.
One lucky matching reading does not establish precision, which requires many repeated readings clustering closely.
A coarse least count tends to reduce precision rather than describe a precise instrument.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Systematic errors differ from random errors mainly because systematic errors:
options: occur unpredictably and are reduced by taking the mean of many readings
always average out to zero over many repeated readings
only occur when the observer misreads the scale
tend to occur consistently in one direction due to a definite cause, such as an instrument's zero error
questions.explanation:
Systematic errors arise from a definite, identifiable cause (such as a zero error, imperfect calibration, or an environmental effect) and bias readings consistently in one direction.

Because they don't vary randomly from trial to trial, they don't cancel out by averaging the way random errors do.
questions.hint: Look for a fixed, repeatable cause behind the error rather than random scatter.
distractor_logic: This describes random errors, not systematic errors.
Random errors tend to average out over many readings; systematic errors do not, since they bias every reading in the same direction.
This describes one narrow example of a personal error, not a general definition of systematic errors.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: How many significant figures are in the number 0.00420?
questions.explanation:
Leading zeros before the first nonzero digit are never significant, so the two zeros right after the decimal point don't count.

The significant digits are 4, 2, and 0 (the trailing zero counts because it comes after the decimal point and after nonzero digits), giving 3 significant figures.
questions.hint: Start counting from the first nonzero digit; a trailing zero after the decimal point still counts.
distractor_logic: Wrongly drops the trailing zero after the 2, even though a trailing zero following the decimal point and nonzero digits is significant.
Counts the two leading zeros before the 4 as significant, along with the three real digits.
Overcounts by treating the decimal point or an extra placeholder as contributing to the digit count.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: How many significant figures are in \(3.0500\times10^4\)?
questions.explanation:
In scientific notation, every digit written in the coefficient is significant.

The coefficient 3.0500 has the digits 3, 0, 5, 0, 0 — all five are significant. The exponent is never counted as a significant figure.
questions.hint: Only the coefficient's digits count; the power of ten never adds to the significant-figure count.
distractor_logic: Counts only the nonzero digits (3 and 5), ignoring that zeros within and at the end of the coefficient are also significant.
Drops only the final trailing zero in the coefficient, treating it as a mere placeholder while still counting the other zeros, undercounting by one.
Wrongly includes the exponent's digit (4) as if it contributed to the count of significant figures.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Which of the following numbers has exactly 4 significant figures?
questions.explanation:
In 0.001200, the leading zeros are not significant, but the two trailing zeros after the decimal point are, since they follow nonzero digits.

The significant digits are 1, 2, 0, 0 — a total of 4.
questions.hint: Trailing zeros after a decimal point are always significant, unlike leading zeros.
distractor_logic: Without a decimal point or scientific notation, trailing zeros in a plain integer are ambiguous and conventionally not counted, giving only 2 significant figures here.
This scientific-notation form carries only 2 significant figures (1 and 2).
The leading zeros are not significant, leaving only 2 significant figures (1 and 2).

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Which digits are never counted as significant figures?
options: trailing zeros that appear after a decimal point
zeros sandwiched between two nonzero digits
the first nonzero digit in a number
leading zeros that appear before the first nonzero digit
questions.explanation:
Leading zeros only fix the position of the decimal point and carry no information about measurement precision, so they are never significant.

Captive zeros (between nonzero digits) and trailing zeros after a decimal point, by contrast, are always significant.
questions.hint: Leading zeros are placeholders, not measured digits.
distractor_logic: These zeros ARE significant when they follow the decimal point, contrary to this claim.
These "captive" zeros are always significant, contrary to this claim.
The first nonzero digit is always significant; in fact it marks the starting point for counting.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: The number 5000, written with no decimal point and no scientific notation, has how many significant figures by standard convention?
questions.explanation:
Without a decimal point, trailing zeros in an integer are ambiguous, so by convention only the nonzero digit(s) are taken as significant.

Here only the digit 5 is unambiguously significant; to show more precision the number should be written as \(5.000\times10^3\) (4 significant figures) or similar.
questions.hint: This ambiguity is exactly why scientific notation is preferred for reporting precision.
distractor_logic: Assumes all the trailing zeros are significant, which would require writing the number with a decimal point or in scientific notation to justify.
Inconsistently treats some but not all of the trailing zeros as significant.
Incorrectly suggests a nonzero number can have no significant figures at all.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Rounding 6.451 to 3 significant figures gives:
questions.explanation:
To keep 3 significant figures, digits after 6.45 must be dropped.

Since the next digit (1) is less than 5, the last retained digit stays the same, giving 6.45.
questions.hint: Look only at the very next digit to decide whether to round up or keep it as is.
distractor_logic: Rounds to only 2 significant figures instead of the requested 3.
Incorrectly rounds up even though the digit being dropped (1) is less than 5.
Keeps 4 significant figures instead of the requested 3.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Rounding 6.455 to 3 significant figures, using the simple round-half-up convention, gives:
questions.explanation:
To keep 3 significant figures in 6.455, the digit 5 must be dropped.

Under the round-half-up convention, a dropped digit of exactly 5 rounds the preceding digit up, so 6.455 becomes 6.46.
questions.hint: Round-half-up always pushes an exact 5 upward, unlike banker's rounding.
distractor_logic: Rounds half down instead of applying the round-half-up convention.
Rounds to only 2 significant figures instead of the requested 3.
Alters a digit that should remain unchanged, instead of correctly rounding at the third significant figure.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Significant figures in a measured number represent:
options: only the digits that are completely certain, excluding any estimated digit
every digit that appears in the number, including all leading zeros
the number of decimal places recorded, regardless of the leading digits
all the digits that are known reliably, plus one uncertain (estimated) digit
questions.explanation:
A measurement's significant figures include every digit known with certainty plus one final digit that is estimated (uncertain) by the observer.

This is why significant figures reflect the precision of the measuring instrument used.
questions.hint: The very last significant digit is always a reasonable estimate, not a certainty.
distractor_logic: This wrongly excludes the one uncertain digit that is conventionally included among the significant figures.
Leading zeros are placeholders that fix the decimal point's position, not reliably known or estimated digits.
Significant figures count meaningful digits overall, which is a different idea from simply counting decimal places.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of force is:
questions.explanation:
Force \(=\) mass \(\times\) acceleration, and acceleration has dimensions \([L^1T^{-2}]\).

So force has dimensions \([M^1]\times[L^1T^{-2}] = [M^1L^1T^{-2}]\).
questions.hint: Start from \(F=ma\) and multiply the dimensions of mass and acceleration.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of energy/work, mistakenly used in place of force's.
Drops the mass dimension entirely, even though force depends on mass through \(F=ma\).
Uses the time exponent of velocity instead of acceleration; force needs \(T^{-2}\), not \(T^{-1}\).

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of a dimensionless quantity such as strain is:
options: it has no dimensional formula at all
the dimensional formula cannot be determined without more information
questions.explanation:
Strain is a ratio of two lengths (change in length over original length), so all its dimensions cancel out.

Its dimensional formula is written as \([M^0L^0T^0]\), not left undefined or given a nonzero exponent.
questions.hint: Dimensionless does not mean 'no formula' — it means every exponent is zero.
distractor_logic: Every physical quantity has a dimensional formula; a dimensionless quantity's formula is \([M^0L^0T^0]\), not an absence of one.
Strain, as a ratio of two lengths, is always exactly dimensionless; no further information is needed.
Invents a nonzero length dimension for a quantity that is actually completely dimensionless.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Which of the following is treated as a fundamental dimension in mechanics, alongside mass and time?
questions.explanation:
In mechanics, mass (M), length (L), and time (T) are the fundamental dimensions.

Velocity, force, and momentum are all derived quantities, expressed by combining these three fundamental dimensions.
questions.hint: Only M, L, and T stand alone in mechanics; everything else is built from them.
distractor_logic: Velocity is a derived dimension, built by combining the fundamental dimensions of length and time.
Force is a derived dimension, built from mass, length, and time.
Momentum is also a derived dimension, built from mass, length, and time.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of work (or energy) is:
questions.explanation:
Work \(=\) force \(\times\) distance, so its dimensions are \([M^1L^1T^{-2}]\times[L^1] = [M^1L^2T^{-2}]\).

Energy shares this same dimensional formula, since work and energy are interconvertible.
questions.hint: Multiply the dimensions of force by the dimension of displacement.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of force, mistakenly used in place of work/energy.
Uses the wrong time exponent; work requires \(T^{-2}\), not \(T^{-1}\).
Drops the mass dimension, even though work depends on mass through force.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of velocity is:
questions.explanation:
Velocity \(=\) displacement \(\div\) time, so its dimensions are \([L^1]\div[T^1] = [M^0L^1T^{-1}]\).

Velocity carries no mass dimension at all.
questions.hint: Velocity is just length divided by time — no mass involved.
distractor_logic: Uses the wrong sign on the time exponent, as though velocity grew with time rather than being distance divided by time.
Wrongly includes a mass dimension; velocity does not depend on mass.
Uses the wrong length exponent, as if velocity were an area-based quantity rather than a simple length-per-time.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Dimensional analysis is chiefly used to:
options: determine the exact numerical value of dimensionless constants in an equation
check whether a physical equation is dimensionally consistent
prove that a dimensionally correct equation is numerically accurate
measure the precise magnitude of a physical quantity
questions.explanation:
Dimensional analysis checks that both sides of an equation have matching dimensions, which is a necessary condition for the equation to be physically valid.

It cannot supply dimensionless numerical constants, and dimensional consistency alone never guarantees an equation is numerically correct.
questions.hint: Think of it as a consistency check, not a way to compute numbers or constants.
distractor_logic: Dimensional analysis can never pin down a pure number like \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) or \(\pi\), since such constants carry no dimensions to analyze.
Dimensional consistency is necessary but not sufficient; a dimensionally correct equation can still be numerically wrong.
Dimensional analysis deals with the dimensional formula of quantities, not with producing a numeric measured value.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The refractive index of a medium has the dimensional formula:
options: it has no dimensional formula, since it is just a ratio
questions.explanation:
Refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in the medium, so the dimensions of speed cancel completely.

Its dimensional formula is \([M^0L^0T^0]\), the standard way to represent any dimensionless quantity.
questions.hint: It's a ratio of two speeds, so every dimension cancels out.
distractor_logic: A ratio of two identical dimensions still has a dimensional formula; here every exponent is zero, \([M^0L^0T^0]\), rather than being undefined.
Invents a nonzero length dimension for a quantity that is actually completely dimensionless.
Invents a nonzero time dimension for a quantity that is actually completely dimensionless.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of density is:
questions.explanation:
Density \(=\) mass \(\div\) volume, and volume has dimensions \([L^3]\).

So density has dimensions \([M^1]\div[L^3] = [M^1L^{-3}T^0]\).
questions.hint: Density is mass divided by volume; volume itself is length cubed.
distractor_logic: Uses the wrong sign on the length exponent; density decreases as volume increases, so the exponent must be negative.
Adds an unnecessary time dimension; density involves only mass and volume, with no time dependence.
Drops the mass dimension entirely, even though density is mass per unit volume.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
questions.explanation:
To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by \(\dfrac{1000}{3600}\), which is the same as dividing by 3.6.

\(72\text{ km/h} = \dfrac{72}{3.6}\text{ m/s} = 20\text{ m/s}\).
questions.hint: Dividing the km/h value by 3.6 is a quick shortcut for this common conversion.
distractor_logic: Converts kilometres to metres (\(\times1000\)) but forgets to also convert hours to seconds.
Multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing by 3.6, inverting the standard km/h-to-m/s conversion factor.
Divides by 60 as if converting to metres per minute, stopping one step short of metres per second.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The SI unit of pressure, pascal, expressed in base units is:
questions.explanation:
Pascal \(=\) newton / metre\(^2\), and newton itself is \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\).

Dividing by \(\text{m}^2\) gives \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}/\text{m}^2 = \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}\).
questions.hint: First express newton in base units, then divide by area (m\(^2\)).
distractor_logic: This is the base-unit expression of newton (force), not of pascal (pressure).
Uses an incorrect length exponent, from miscounting the division by area.
Uses an incorrect time exponent, dropping one power of inverse time.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Which combination correctly expresses the SI unit of electric charge in terms of base units?
questions.explanation:
Electric charge \(=\) current \(\times\) time.

So its base-unit expression is ampere \(\times\) second, written as A\(\cdot\)s (equivalently, the coulomb).
questions.hint: Charge builds from current the same way distance builds from speed: quantity \(\times\) time.
distractor_logic: Inverts the relationship; charge is current multiplied by time, not divided by time.
Uses an incorrect time exponent; charge involves only one power of time, not two.
Adds an unnecessary mass unit; electric charge involves only current and time.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert a density of 1 g/cm\(^3\) into kg/m\(^3\).
questions.hint: Convert the mass and volume units separately, then combine the two factors.
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert at all, treating the numerical value in g/cm\(^3\) as if it were already in kg/m\(^3\).
Inverts the conversion factor, dividing by 1000 instead of multiplying by 1000.
Uses a conversion factor of 100 instead of the correct 1000.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The SI unit of angular velocity, expressed in base units, is:
questions.explanation: Angular velocity \(=\) angle \(\div\) time. Since radian is a dimensionless supplementary unit, angular velocity in base units reduces to \(\text{s}^{-1}\), usually still labeled rad/s for clarity.
questions.hint: Radian carries no dimension of its own, so it drops out when expressing this in base units.
distractor_logic: Confuses angular velocity (angle per time) with linear velocity (length per time).
Omits the per-time dependence entirely; angular velocity is angle divided by time, not angle alone.
Inverts the time exponent, giving a unit of time rather than an inverse-time rate.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: One light year is approximately \(9.46\times10^{15}\) m. Expressed in kilometres, this is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Since 1 km \(= 10^3\) m, dividing the metre value by \(10^3\) gives the value in kilometres.

\(9.46\times10^{15}\text{ m} \div 10^3 = 9.46\times10^{12}\text{ km}\).
questions.hint: Dividing by \(10^3\) shifts the exponent down by exactly 3.
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert metres to kilometres at all, keeping the same power of ten.
Multiplies by 1000 instead of dividing by 1000 when converting metres to kilometres.
Divides by \(10^{6}\) instead of \(10^{3}\) when converting metres to kilometres.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The unit kilowatt-hour (kWh), commonly used for electricity billing, is dimensionally equivalent to the SI unit:
questions.explanation:
Power \(\times\) time \(=\) energy, and kilowatt-hour is exactly kilowatt (power) \(\times\) hour (time).

So a kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, dimensionally equivalent to the joule, even though it is not itself an SI unit.
questions.hint: Multiplying a power unit by a time unit always yields an energy unit.
distractor_logic: Kilowatt-hour includes an extra time factor beyond kilowatt, making it a unit of energy, not power.
Kilowatt-hour has no direct dimensional relationship to force.
Kilowatt-hour has no dimensional relationship to pressure.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert 3 tonnes (metric tons) into kilograms.
questions.explanation:
1 tonne \(= 1000\) kg.

So \(3\text{ tonnes} = 3\times1000\text{ kg} = 3000\text{ kg}\).
questions.hint: A tonne is a thousand kilograms, similar to how a kilometre is a thousand metres.
distractor_logic: Uses a conversion factor of 100 instead of the correct 1000 for tonnes to kilograms.
Introduces an extra factor of 10, using 10000 instead of the correct 1000.
Treats tonne and kilogram as if they were the same unit.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A vernier caliper with least count 0.01 cm gives a main scale reading of 3.4 cm, with the 6th vernier division coinciding with a main scale line. The total reading is:
questions.explanation:
Total reading \(=\) main scale reading \(+\) (coinciding vernier division number \(\times\) least count).

\(= 3.4 + (6\times0.01) = 3.4 + 0.06 = 3.46\) cm.
questions.hint: Multiply the coinciding division number by the least count before adding it on.
distractor_logic: Ignores the vernier scale contribution entirely, reporting only the main scale reading.
Misplaces the vernier contribution as if it added a tenths digit instead of the correct hundredths digit.
Adds the raw vernier division number (6) directly as tenths of a centimetre, instead of first scaling it by the least count.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale (no zero error). The main scale reading is 2 mm and the circular scale reading is 20 divisions. The measured diameter is:
questions.explanation:
Least count \(=\dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{circular divisions}} = \dfrac{0.5}{50} = 0.01\) mm.

Diameter \(=\) main scale reading \(+\) (circular scale reading \(\times\) least count) \(= 2 + (20\times0.01) = 2.2\) mm.
questions.hint: Compute the least count first, then multiply it by the circular scale reading.
distractor_logic: Uses an incorrect least count of 0.001 mm (as if there were 500 circular divisions) instead of the correct 0.01 mm.
Forgets to scale the circular scale reading by the least count, simply adding the raw division count to the main scale reading.
Adds the pitch value directly to the main scale reading, ignoring the circular scale reading altogether.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A vernier caliper has a positive zero error of \(+0.02\) cm. The observed reading of an object's length is 4.56 cm. The corrected (true) length is:
questions.explanation:
For a positive zero error, the true reading is obtained by subtracting the zero error from the observed reading.

True length \(= 4.56 - 0.02 = 4.54\) cm.
questions.hint: A positive zero error always makes the instrument over-read, so subtract it.
distractor_logic: Adds the zero error instead of subtracting it, the reverse of the correct correction for a positive zero error.
Ignores the zero error entirely, reporting the raw observed reading as the true value.
Misapplies the zero error, adding 0.04 cm instead of subtracting the stated 0.02 cm.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A screw gauge has a negative zero error of \(-0.03\) mm. The observed reading is 1.20 mm. The corrected (true) reading is:
questions.explanation:
For a negative zero error, the true reading is obtained by subtracting the (negative) zero error, which is the same as adding its magnitude.

True reading \(= 1.20 - (-0.03) = 1.20 + 0.03 = 1.23\) mm.
questions.hint: Subtracting a negative zero error means adding its magnitude back.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the magnitude of the zero error as though it were positive, instead of adding it back for a negative zero error.
Ignores the zero error entirely, reporting the raw observed reading as the true value.
Adds twice the zero error's magnitude by mistake instead of adding it once.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A vernier caliper's main scale has divisions of 0.5 mm, and 25 vernier divisions coincide with 24 main-scale divisions. The least count is:
questions.hint: First find the value of one vernier division as a fraction of the main-scale division.
distractor_logic: Off by one decimal place, from mishandling the millimetre-to-centimetre conversion at the end.
Reports the main-scale division value directly, without subtracting the value of one vernier division.
Reports the value of one vernier-scale division itself, instead of computing the least count as the difference from one main-scale division.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: To find the volume of a small, irregularly shaped stone, the most suitable technique is to use:
options: a vernier caliper, measuring the stone's length, breadth, and height directly
a graduated measuring cylinder, noting the rise in water level when the stone is submerged
a screw gauge, measuring the stone's diameter
a spring balance, reading the extension it produces
questions.explanation:
For an irregular solid, volume is best found by liquid displacement: the rise in water level in a graduated cylinder directly equals the volume of the submerged object.

Linear instruments like a vernier caliper or screw gauge require a regular geometric shape to convert length measurements into a volume formula.
questions.hint: An irregular shape has no simple formula linking length to volume; displacement sidesteps that problem.
distractor_logic: An irregular shape has no well-defined length, breadth, and height to combine into a simple volume formula.
A screw gauge suits small, fairly uniform circular cross-sections like wires, not an irregular solid, and a single diameter can't yield the stone's volume.
A spring balance measures weight (a force), not volume, and gives no direct volume information here.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: Measuring a wire's diameter with a screw gauge at four different points gives 1.20 mm, 1.22 mm, 1.19 mm, and 1.21 mm. This spread most likely arises because:
options: the screw gauge's zero error changes randomly between trials
the student's reaction time varies between readings
the wire's cross-section is not perfectly uniform along its length, so genuine diameter variation exists at different points
the pitch of the screw gauge changes with each rotation
questions.explanation:
Since the four readings were taken at different points along the wire, genuine physical variation in the wire's cross-section is the most natural explanation for the spread.

This is why multiple diameter readings at different points are averaged for a more representative value.
questions.hint: The readings were taken at different locations on the wire, not repeated at the same spot.
distractor_logic: Zero error is a fixed instrumental offset for a given screw gauge and does not fluctuate between trials on the same instrument.
Reaction time affects timing measurements, such as with a stopwatch, not a static length reading taken with a screw gauge.
Pitch is a fixed mechanical property of the instrument and does not vary between measurements.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A student needs the thickness of a single sheet of paper, too thin to read reliably on a screw gauge alone. A good technique is to:
options: measure just one sheet very slowly and carefully with the same screw gauge
use a metre scale instead, since it has larger divisions
measure the sheet's length and width instead of its thickness
stack many identical sheets together, measure the total thickness, and divide by the number of sheets
questions.explanation:
Stacking many identical sheets multiplies the total thickness to a size the screw gauge can resolve reliably.

Dividing the total thickness by the number of sheets then gives an accurate value for a single sheet, effectively improving the instrument's usable precision.
questions.hint: Multiplying a too-small quantity by a known count, then dividing back, is a common precision trick.
distractor_logic: Going slowly does not overcome the instrument's least count limitation on a single very thin sheet.
A metre scale's much coarser least count makes it even less suitable for this precision measurement.
Length and width do not give the thickness the student actually needs to determine.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: If \(Z=AB\), and the percentage errors in A and B are 2% and 3% respectively, the percentage error in Z is:
questions.explanation:
For \(Z=AB\), fractional (percentage) errors always add: \(\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z}=\dfrac{\Delta A}{A}+\dfrac{\Delta B}{B}\).

So the percentage error in Z is \(2\% + 3\% = 5\%\).
questions.hint: For a product, the percentage errors of the two factors simply add together.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two percentage errors instead of adding them, wrongly assuming the errors partially cancel.
Multiplies the two percentage errors together instead of adding them.
Averages the two percentage errors instead of adding them.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: If \(Z=A/B\), and the percentage errors in A and B are 4% and 1% respectively, the percentage error in Z is:
questions.explanation:
For \(Z=A/B\), fractional (percentage) errors always add, even for division: \(\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z}=\dfrac{\Delta A}{A}+\dfrac{\Delta B}{B}\).

So the percentage error in Z is \(4\% + 1\% = 5\%\).
questions.hint: Division never subtracts errors — they still add, just like in multiplication.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the percentage errors, wrongly assuming errors partially cancel in a division.
Ignores the error contributed by B (the denominator) entirely.
Ignores the error contributed by A (the numerator), using only B's error.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: If \(Z=A^3\), and the percentage error in A is 2%, the percentage error in Z is:
questions.explanation:
For \(Z=A^n\), the relative error is scaled by the power: \(\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z}=n\dfrac{\Delta A}{A}\).

So the percentage error in Z is \(3\times2\% = 6\%\).
questions.hint: A power multiplies the relative error by the exponent — it doesn't just copy it over.
distractor_logic: Treats the power the same as a simple product or quotient case, forgetting to multiply by the exponent.
Cubes the percentage-error value itself (\(2^3=8\)) instead of multiplying it by the exponent.
Adds the exponent to the percentage error (\(3+2=5\)) instead of multiplying them.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: If \(Z=A+B\), with absolute errors \(\Delta A = 0.2\) and \(\Delta B = 0.3\) (same units), the absolute error in Z is:
questions.explanation:
For \(Z=A+B\), absolute errors always add: \(\Delta Z=\Delta A+\Delta B\).

So \(\Delta Z = 0.2+0.3=0.5\).
questions.hint: Absolute errors add for a sum, in the same units as the measured quantities.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the absolute errors instead of adding them, wrongly assuming they partially cancel.
Multiplies the two absolute errors instead of adding them.
Averages the two absolute errors instead of adding them.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: If \(Z=A-B\), with absolute errors \(\Delta A = 0.15\) and \(\Delta B = 0.10\), the absolute error in Z is:
questions.explanation:
For \(Z=A-B\), absolute errors always add, even though the quantities themselves are subtracted: \(\Delta Z=\Delta A+\Delta B\).

So \(\Delta Z = 0.15+0.10=0.25\).
questions.hint: Subtraction of quantities never subtracts their errors — the errors still add.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two absolute errors, wrongly assuming errors cancel when the underlying quantities are subtracted.
Reports only the error in A, ignoring the error contributed by B.
Reports only the error in B, ignoring the error contributed by A.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: The length of a rod is measured as 25.4 cm with a possible absolute error of 0.1 cm. The percentage error in this measurement is approximately:
questions.explanation: Percentage error \(=\dfrac{\Delta L}{L}\times100 = \dfrac{0.1}{25.4}\times100 \approx 0.39\%\).
questions.hint: Divide the absolute error by the measured value before multiplying by 100.
distractor_logic: Misplaces a decimal point, off by a factor of 10 from the correct value.
Effectively swaps numerator and denominator, treating the measured length itself as if it were the percentage error.
Uses the absolute error's digits directly as a percentage, without dividing by the measured value first.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Student A measures g as 9.79, 9.81, 9.80, 9.78 m/s\(^2\) (mean 9.795). Student B measures 9.5, 10.1, 9.6, 10.0 m/s\(^2\) (mean 9.8) across four trials each. Which statement is correct?
options: Student B's readings are more precise, since the mean is numerically a rounder number
Both students have equal precision, since their means are nearly the same
Student A's readings are more precise, since they cluster far more tightly together, even though both students have a similar mean
Student A's readings are less precise, since one value (9.78) is below the mean
questions.explanation:
Precision depends on how closely repeated readings cluster together, not on where their mean happens to lie.

Student A's readings span only 0.03 m/s\(^2\), while Student B's span 0.6 m/s\(^2\) — a far wider spread — so Student A's measurements are clearly more precise.
questions.hint: Compare the spread (range) of each student's readings, not just their means.
distractor_logic: A mean being a round number has nothing to do with precision, which depends on how tightly the individual readings cluster.
Similar means relate only to possible accuracy, not to precision, which depends on the spread among individual readings.
A single value lying on either side of the mean says nothing about overall clustering; A's four values are still far more tightly grouped than B's.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: One student reports a pendulum's time period as "T = 2.145 s" from a single unrepeated trial, while another reports "T = 2.1 \(\pm\) 0.1 s" after averaging five trials. Which statement correctly compares these reports?
options: the first report is more meaningful, because more decimal places imply finer precision
both reports are equally meaningful, since they describe the same underlying measurement
the first report is more meaningful, because a single careful reading avoids introducing random errors from repetition
the second report is more meaningful, because it honestly reflects the actual measurement uncertainty, even with fewer decimal digits
questions.explanation:
A stated uncertainty, built from multiple trials, gives a far more honest and useful picture of measurement reliability than an unrepeated reading with many decimal digits.

Decimal digits alone don't guarantee precision; only repeated measurement and honest error reporting do.
questions.hint: More decimal places from a single trial can be misleading rather than genuinely more precise.
distractor_logic: Extra decimal digits from a single, unrepeated trial don't represent genuine precision — they can create a false sense of accuracy.
A report with no stated uncertainty and only one trial is less reliable than an averaged result with an honest error estimate.
Repeating trials and averaging is precisely the standard technique used to reduce, not introduce, the effect of random errors.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Add 12.34 cm and 6.7 cm, reporting the sum to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
In addition, the result's number of decimal places is limited by the term with the fewest decimal places.

6.7 has 1 decimal place while 12.34 has 2, so the sum \(12.34+6.7=19.04\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place, giving 19.0 cm.
questions.hint: Count decimal places, not significant figures, for an addition.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, applying the multiplication rule's significant-figure-count logic instead of the addition rule, which is limited by the fewest decimal places among the terms.
Rounds too aggressively, dropping to zero decimal places instead of the correct one decimal place.
Pads extra unjustified decimal places beyond what either term actually supports.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Multiply 4.5 and 2.10 (both measured values), reporting the product to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
In multiplication, the result's number of significant figures is limited by the factor with the fewest significant figures.

4.5 has 2 significant figures while 2.10 has 3, so the raw product \(4.5\times2.10=9.45\) must be rounded to 2 significant figures, giving 9.5.
questions.hint: Count significant figures, not decimal places, for a multiplication.
distractor_logic: Keeps 3 significant figures, applying the addition/subtraction decimal-place rule instead of the multiplication rule, which is limited by the fewest significant figures among the factors.
Rounds too aggressively, dropping to only 1 significant figure.
Pads extra unjustified significant figures beyond what either factor actually supports.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Subtract 2.13 g from 45.6 g, reporting the result to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
In subtraction, the result's number of decimal places is limited by the term with the fewest decimal places.

45.6 has 1 decimal place while 2.13 has 2, so the raw difference \(45.6-2.13=43.47\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place, giving 43.5 g.
questions.hint: As with addition, subtraction is governed by decimal places, not significant figures.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, applying the multiplication rule's significant-figure-count logic instead of the subtraction rule, which is limited by the fewest decimal places among the terms.
Rounds too aggressively, dropping to zero decimal places instead of the correct one decimal place.
Pads extra unjustified decimal places beyond what either term actually supports.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Divide 15.0 by 3.0 (both measured values), reporting the quotient to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
In division, the result's number of significant figures is limited by the value with the fewest significant figures.

Both 15.0 and 3.0 have 2 significant figures, so the quotient must also carry 2 significant figures: 5.0.
questions.hint: Even though 15.0/3.0 works out to exactly 5, the reported answer must still reflect 2 significant figures.
distractor_logic: Drops to only 1 significant figure, understating the precision the data actually justifies.
Pads an extra unjustified significant figure beyond what either value actually supports.
Pads several extra unjustified significant figures, treating the division as though it were exact.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Add 3.6 m, 4.25 m, and 0.048 m, reporting the sum to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
The decimal places are 1 (3.6), 2 (4.25), and 3 (0.048); the least of these is 1 decimal place.

The raw sum \(3.6+4.25+0.048=7.898\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place, giving 7.9 m.
questions.hint: The single term with the fewest decimal places sets the limit for the whole sum, even with three terms.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, matching the second-most restrictive term instead of the single most restrictive (fewest-decimal-place) term.
Keeps every decimal place from the raw sum without applying any rounding rule.
Rounds too aggressively to zero decimal places.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Multiply 2.4, 3.65, and 1.2 (all measured values), reporting the product to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
The significant figures are 2 (2.4), 3 (3.65), and 2 (1.2); the least of these is 2 significant figures.

The raw product \(2.4\times3.65\times1.2=10.512\) must be rounded to 2 significant figures, giving 11.
questions.hint: The term with the fewest significant figures caps the precision of the whole product, even with three factors.
distractor_logic: Keeps 3 significant figures, matching the term with the most significant figures instead of the fewest.
Keeps 4 significant figures, essentially reporting the raw product without any rounding at all.
Rounds to only 1 significant figure, underestimating what the least-precise term (2 significant figures) actually justifies.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Compute \(8.0\text{ cm} - 3.0\text{ cm} + 1.25\text{ cm}\), reporting the answer to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
8.0 and 3.0 each have 1 decimal place while 1.25 has 2, so the least is 1 decimal place.

The raw result \(8.0-3.0+1.25=6.25\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place; since the dropped digit is exactly 5, round-half-up gives 6.3 cm.
questions.hint: Find the minimum decimal-place count across all the terms in the whole expression first.
distractor_logic: Reports 2 decimal places, matching the most precise term instead of the least precise term.
Rounds half down instead of applying the round-half-up convention on the final digit.
Rounds too aggressively to zero decimal places.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between the significant-figure rules for addition/subtraction and for multiplication/division?
options: both operations require matching the term with the fewest significant figures
both operations require matching the term with the fewest decimal places
addition/subtraction matches significant figures while multiplication/division matches decimal places
addition/subtraction keeps as many decimal places as the least precise term; multiplication/division keeps as many significant figures as the term with the fewest significant figures
questions.explanation:
Addition and subtraction results are limited by the fewest decimal places among the terms, since decimal place reflects the absolute precision of each measurement.

Multiplication and division results are instead limited by the fewest significant figures among the factors, since relative precision is what matters there.
questions.hint: Decimal places govern addition and subtraction; significant-figure counts govern multiplication and division.
distractor_logic: This rule applies only to multiplication/division; addition and subtraction are instead governed by matching decimal places.
This rule applies only to addition/subtraction; multiplication and division are instead governed by matching significant-figure counts.
This states the two rules exactly backwards from how they actually work.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Check the dimensional consistency of \(v = u + at\), where v and u are velocities, a is acceleration, and t is time.
options: the equation is dimensionally consistent, since every term has dimensions \([M^0L^1T^{-1}]\)
the equation is dimensionally inconsistent, since \(at\) has different dimensions from \(v\) and \(u\)
the equation is consistent, but only because velocity and acceleration share the same dimensional formula
the equation cannot be checked dimensionally since it contains addition
questions.explanation:
\([v]=[u]=[M^0L^1T^{-1}]\), and \([at]=[L^1T^{-2}]\times[T^1]=[M^0L^1T^{-1}]\).

Since all three terms carry identical dimensions, the equation is dimensionally consistent.
questions.hint: Check that every term added together shares the exact same dimensional formula.
distractor_logic: \(at\) has dimensions \([L^1T^{-2}]\times[T^1]=[L^1T^{-1}]\), which exactly matches v and u; this claim of mismatch is false.
Velocity and acceleration do not share the same dimensional formula at all; the equation's consistency does not depend on any such coincidence.
Dimensional analysis can absolutely check equations with addition, as long as every added term shares matching dimensions.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Check whether \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) is dimensionally consistent (s: displacement, u: velocity, a: acceleration, t: time).
options: no, because the \(\frac{1}{2}\) factor is not dimensionless and disrupts the balance
yes, dimensionally consistent — every term reduces to \([M^0L^1T^0]\)
no, because \(ut\) has different dimensions from \(\frac{1}{2}at^2\)
cannot be determined without knowing the numerical values of u, a, and t
questions.explanation:
\([ut]=[L^1T^{-1}]\times[T^1]=[L^1]\), and \([at^2]=[L^1T^{-2}]\times[T^2]=[L^1]\), matching \([s]=[L^1]\).

Numerical constants like \(\tfrac12\) never carry dimensions, so they never affect this check. The equation is dimensionally consistent.
questions.hint: A pure number like \(\tfrac12\) is always dimensionless and can be ignored in a dimensional check.
distractor_logic: The numerical factor \(\tfrac12\) is a pure, dimensionless number and never affects a dimensional check.
Both terms actually reduce to the same dimension, \([L^1]\); this claim of mismatch is false.
Dimensional consistency depends only on the dimensional formulae of the quantities involved, never on their numerical values.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: A pendulum's time period is proposed as \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}\), where l is length and g is acceleration due to gravity. What does dimensional analysis show?
options: the formula is dimensionally inconsistent, since g involves an inverse time-squared dimension
the formula is dimensionally consistent, and this alone proves the constant \(2\pi\) is numerically correct
the formula is dimensionally consistent, though dimensional analysis alone could never have derived the numerical factor \(2\pi\) from scratch
dimensional analysis cannot be applied here because of the square root
questions.explanation:
\(\left[\dfrac{l}{g}\right]=\dfrac{L^1}{L^1T^{-2}}=T^2\), so \(\left[\sqrt{l/g}\right]=T^1\), matching \([T]\) for time period.

The formula checks out dimensionally, but the exact value of \(2\pi\) is a separate, purely numerical result that dimensional analysis cannot supply or verify on its own.
questions.hint: Dimensional analysis confirms consistency, but it can never pin down a pure numerical constant.
distractor_logic: This reasoning is flawed; g's \(T^{-2}\) exactly cancels correctly once combined with l and the square root, leaving a clean \([T^1]\).
Dimensional consistency can never verify a dimensionless numerical constant like \(2\pi\); it only checks that the dimensions on both sides balance.
Dimensional analysis works perfectly well with roots and powers, as long as fractional dimensional exponents are tracked consistently.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: The dimensional formula of angular momentum is:
questions.explanation: Angular momentum \(= mvr\), so its dimensions are \([M^1]\times[L^1T^{-1}]\times[L^1] = [M^1L^2T^{-1}]\).
questions.hint: Angular momentum is linear momentum multiplied by a radius — one extra factor of length.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of linear momentum, mistakenly used in place of angular momentum's.
This is the dimensional formula of energy, mistakenly used in place of angular momentum's.
Drops the mass dimension entirely, even though angular momentum depends on mass through linear momentum.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: From \(F=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\), the dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant G is:
questions.explanation: Rearranging, \(G=\dfrac{Fr^2}{m_1m_2}\), with dimensions \(\dfrac{[M^1L^1T^{-2}]\times[L^2]}{[M^2]} = [M^{-1}L^{3}T^{-2}]\).
questions.hint: Rearrange the formula to isolate G first, then substitute each quantity's dimensions.
distractor_logic: Uses the wrong sign on the mass exponent, forgetting that G is obtained by dividing by \(m_1m_2\), not multiplying by it.
Uses the wrong length exponent, from mishandling the division by \(r^2\).
Uses the wrong time exponent, borrowed from force's formula without correctly tracking the full rearrangement.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: From \(E=h\nu\), where E is energy and \(\nu\) is frequency, the dimensional formula of Planck's constant h is:
questions.explanation: Rearranging, \(h = E/\nu\), with dimensions \(\dfrac{[M^1L^2T^{-2}]}{[T^{-1}]} = [M^1L^2T^{-1}]\).
questions.hint: Frequency has dimensions \([T^{-1}]\); dividing energy's dimensions by this flips its sign in the exponent.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of energy itself, forgetting to divide by the dimensions of frequency.
Uses the wrong length exponent, mistakenly matching linear momentum's formula instead.
