Forgets the inverse-time dimension entirely, treating frequency as though it were dimensionless.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Surface tension is defined as force per unit length. Its dimensional formula is:
questions.explanation: Surface tension \(=\dfrac{\text{force}}{\text{length}}\), with dimensions \(\dfrac{[M^1L^1T^{-2}]}{[L^1]} = [M^1L^0T^{-2}]\).
questions.hint: Dividing force's dimensions by length cancels exactly one power of L.
distractor_logic: This is the dimensional formula of force itself, forgetting to divide by the length dimension.
Uses the wrong length exponent, as though dividing by length squared instead of length.
Drops the mass dimension entirely, even though surface tension is derived from force, which includes mass.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Coefficient of friction, the ratio of frictional force to normal force, is a physical quantity that is:
options: measured in newtons, the same unit as force
impossible to assign a dimensional formula to, since it depends on surface roughness
questions.explanation:
Since coefficient of friction is the ratio of two forces, all dimensions cancel completely.

Its dimensional formula is \([M^0L^0T^0]\), the standard way of representing a dimensionless quantity — not "no formula" and not some invented nonzero dimension.
questions.hint: Any ratio of two quantities with identical dimensions is always dimensionless.
distractor_logic: Coefficient of friction is a pure ratio of two forces, so it carries no units at all, unlike force itself.
This invents a nonzero dimension for a quantity that is actually completely dimensionless.
Depending on surface properties affects only its numerical value, not whether a dimensional formula exists; as a ratio of two forces it is always \([M^0L^0T^0]\).

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert a pressure of \(1.013\times10^5\) Pa (1 atm) into dyne/cm\(^2\) (CGS units), given \(1\text{ Pa} = 10\) dyne/cm\(^2\).
questions.explanation: Multiplying by the given conversion factor: \(1.013\times10^5\text{ Pa}\times10\text{ (dyne/cm}^2\text{ per Pa)} = 1.013\times10^6\) dyne/cm\(^2\).
questions.hint: Just multiply the given pressure by the stated conversion factor of 10.
distractor_logic: Forgets to apply the Pa-to-dyne/cm\(^2\) conversion factor at all, simply keeping the same numerical value.
Inverts the conversion factor, dividing by 10 instead of multiplying by 10.
Uses a conversion factor of 100 instead of the correct factor of 10 between Pa and dyne/cm\(^2\).

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: A nuclear reaction releases 3.2 MeV of energy. Convert this into joules, given \(1\text{ eV} = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) J.
questions.explanation:
First convert MeV to eV: \(3.2\text{ MeV} = 3.2\times10^6\) eV.

Then convert to joules: \(3.2\times10^6\times1.6\times10^{-19} = 5.12\times10^{-13}\) J.
questions.hint: This is a two-step conversion: MeV to eV first, then eV to joules.
distractor_logic: Forgets to first convert MeV to eV (a factor of \(10^6\)) before applying the eV-to-joule conversion.
Combines the two required powers of ten incorrectly, producing the wrong overall exponent.
Omits multiplying by 3.2 entirely, using only the base eV-to-joule conversion constant as the final answer.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The Stefan–Boltzmann constant \(\sigma\) has SI units \(\text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}\). Expressed fully in base SI units, this is:
questions.explanation:
Watt in base units is \(\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-3}\).

So \(\text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4} = \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-3}\times\text{m}^{-2}\times\text{K}^{-4} = \text{kg s}^{-3}\text{K}^{-4}\), since the \(\text{m}^2\) and \(\text{m}^{-2}\) exactly cancel.
questions.hint: Expand watt into base units first, then combine the length exponents carefully.
distractor_logic: Forgets to cancel the \(\text{m}^2\) from watt against the \(\text{m}^{-2}\) already present, leaving an uncancelled length dimension.
Cancels the length dimension incorrectly, leaving a residual \(\text{m}^{-2}\) instead of no length dimension at all.
Drops three powers of the temperature dimension, using \(\text{K}^{-1}\) instead of the correct \(\text{K}^{-4}\).

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: A star's luminosity is \(3.8\times10^{26}\) W. Express this in erg/s (CGS units), given \(1\text{ W} = 10^7\) erg/s.
questions.explanation: Multiplying by the given conversion factor: \(3.8\times10^{26}\times10^7 = 3.8\times10^{33}\) erg/s.
questions.hint: Adding the exponents \(26+7\) gives the correct power of ten.
distractor_logic: Forgets to apply the watt-to-erg/s conversion factor at all.
Inverts the conversion factor, dividing by \(10^7\) instead of multiplying by it.
Uses a conversion factor of \(10^4\) instead of the correct \(10^7\).

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Convert a pressure of 750 mmHg into pascals, given \(1\text{ mmHg}\approx133.3\) Pa.
questions.explanation: \(750\times133.3 \approx 9.998\times10^4\) Pa, close to the standard atmospheric pressure of about \(1.0\times10^5\) Pa.
questions.hint: Multiply the mmHg value directly by the given Pa-per-mmHg factor.
distractor_logic: Reports the conversion factor itself rather than the fully converted pressure value.
Forgets to apply the mmHg-to-pascal conversion factor at all, treating the two numerical values as directly interchangeable.
Introduces an extra unintended factor of 100 during the multiplication.

questions.topic: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: The specific heat capacity of water, 4184 J kg\(^{-1}\)K\(^{-1}\), expressed in CGS units (erg g\(^{-1}\)K\(^{-1}\)) using \(1\text{ J}=10^7\) erg and \(1\text{ kg}=10^3\) g, becomes:
questions.explanation:
Converting joules to ergs multiplies by \(10^7\); converting per-kilogram to per-gram divides by \(10^3\).

\(4184\times\dfrac{10^7}{10^3} = 4184\times10^4 = 4.184\times10^7\) erg g\(^{-1}\)K\(^{-1}\).
questions.hint: Apply the energy-unit conversion and the mass-unit conversion as two separate factors.
distractor_logic: Multiplies both conversion factors together instead of dividing by the mass conversion factor, effectively squaring its effect.
Applies only the mass conversion (kg to g) and forgets to also convert joules to ergs.
Forgets to apply either conversion factor, simply relabeling the original units.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A screw gauge (pitch 1 mm, 100 circular divisions) has a positive zero error of 4 divisions. For an object, the main scale reading is 3 mm and the circular scale reading is 45 divisions. Find the true diameter.
questions.explanation:
Least count \(=\dfrac{1\text{ mm}}{100}=0.01\) mm, so the zero error \(= 4\times0.01 = 0.04\) mm.

Observed reading \(= 3+(45\times0.01)=3.45\) mm.

True reading \(=\) observed \(-\) zero error \(= 3.45-0.04=3.41\) mm.
questions.hint: Convert the zero-error division count into a length using the least count before subtracting it.
distractor_logic: Ignores the zero error entirely, reporting the raw observed reading as the true value.
Adds the zero error instead of subtracting it, the reverse of the correct correction for a positive zero error.
Miscalculates the zero error's length value using the wrong least count (0.1 mm instead of the correct 0.01 mm), so subtracts 0.4 mm instead of 0.04 mm.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A vernier caliper has 20 vernier divisions coinciding with 19 main-scale divisions (main scale smallest division 1 mm), and a negative zero error of 2 divisions. An object's observed reading is 5.34 cm. Find the true length.
questions.explanation:
1 VSD \(=\dfrac{19}{20}\text{ mm}=0.95\) mm, so least count \(= 1-0.95=0.05\) mm \(=0.005\) cm.

Zero error \(=-2\times0.005=-0.01\) cm.

True length \(=\) observed \(-\) zero error \(= 5.34-(-0.01)=5.35\) cm.
questions.hint: Compute the least count carefully first, since this vernier's division ratio isn't the usual 10-to-9.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the zero error's magnitude as though it were a positive zero error, instead of adding it back for a negative zero error.
Ignores the zero error entirely, reporting the raw observed reading as the true value.
Uses an incorrect least count (as if 10 vernier divisions matched 9 main-scale divisions, giving 0.01 cm) instead of the correctly computed 0.005 cm, overstating the zero-error correction.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A student must measure the length of a table (about 1.5 m) and the diameter of a small ball bearing (about 4 mm) in the same experiment. Which pairing of instruments is most appropriate?
options: a metre scale for the table's length, and a screw gauge for the ball bearing's diameter
a screw gauge for both measurements
a vernier caliper for both measurements
a metre scale for both measurements
questions.explanation:
Instrument choice depends on matching both the range and the required precision to the object being measured.

A metre scale suits the table's large length, while a screw gauge's much finer least count suits the ball bearing's small diameter — no single instrument here fits both jobs well.
questions.hint: Match each instrument's range and least count to the size of what's actually being measured.
distractor_logic: A screw gauge's jaws and scale range are far too small to span a length as large as 1.5 m.
A typical vernier caliper's range (often well under half a metre) cannot span a 1.5 m table length, even though it could handle the ball bearing.
A metre scale's least count, about 1 mm, is far too coarse to meaningfully resolve a 4 mm ball bearing's diameter.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A screw gauge shows backlash error (the screw does not advance immediately when the direction of rotation is reversed). The recommended technique to avoid this error during a measurement is to:
options: apply extra force when closing the jaws to compensate for the lost motion
always rotate the screw in the same direction while closing in on the object, never reversing direction mid-measurement
always take the reading with the screw fully open before closing it around the object
double the pitch value to compensate for the expected error
questions.explanation:
Backlash error arises from small looseness in the screw mechanism when its rotation direction is reversed.

Always turning the screw in one consistent direction while closing on the object avoids engaging that lost motion, sidestepping the error entirely.
questions.hint: The fix is about the direction of turning, not about force or the scale's numbers.
distractor_logic: Extra force can damage the object or the instrument and does not correctly compensate for the lost mechanical motion caused by backlash.
This alone does not avoid the internal lost motion in the screw threads; it is the direction of approach mid-measurement that matters.
Modifying the pitch value has nothing to do with correcting for backlash, which is a mechanical issue in how the screw is turned, not a scale-reading issue.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: While reading a metre scale, a student's eye is positioned obliquely (not directly perpendicular) above the scale markings. This is most likely to introduce:
options: a zero error, since the scale's starting point has shifted
a random error that cannot be traced to any specific cause
a parallax error, causing the reading to appear shifted from its true position on the scale
an increase in the instrument's least count
questions.explanation:
Viewing a scale from an angle rather than directly above the marking shifts the apparent position of the pointer or edge relative to the scale, a classic parallax error.

This is avoided by always positioning the eye directly perpendicular to the scale while reading.
questions.hint: This is the same effect that makes a car's speedometer needle look different depending on the driver's eye position.
distractor_logic: Zero error is a fixed instrumental offset present even before any reading is taken; it has nothing to do with the observer's eye position during a specific reading.
An oblique line of sight is a definite, identifiable cause, making this closer to a systematic-type error rather than an untraceable random one.
Least count is a fixed property of the instrument's construction and does not change based on how the observer positions their eye.

questions.topic: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A student measures the same length five times with a vernier caliper (least count 0.01 cm), getting 4.52, 4.53, 4.52, 4.54, 4.52 cm. This small scatter is best explained by:
options: a large systematic zero error affecting every reading equally
the vernier caliper's pitch being incorrectly manufactured
the object's length physically changing between each trial
small random variations in reading the vernier coincidence and object placement, combined with the instrument's finite least count
questions.explanation:
Such small, non-repeating differences between trials, comparable to just a few least counts, are the signature of random errors — small unavoidable variations in reading and placement.

This is exactly why taking the mean of several trials gives a more reliable value than any single reading.
questions.hint: Differences this small, that don't repeat in a fixed pattern, point to random rather than systematic causes.
distractor_logic: A zero error shifts every reading by the same fixed amount, which would not explain readings differing from each other.
Pitch is a screw-gauge property, not a vernier-caliper property, and a manufacturing defect isn't the typical explanation for this kind of small everyday reading scatter.
A rigid solid object's length does not change between repeated measurements taken moments apart.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Kinetic energy is calculated using \(KE=\frac{1}{2}mv^2\). If mass is measured with 1% error and velocity with 2% error, the percentage error in the calculated kinetic energy is:
questions.explanation:
\(KE\propto m^1v^2\), so its relative error is \(1\times(\text{error in }m) + 2\times(\text{error in }v)\).

\(= (1\times1\%) + (2\times2\%) = 1\%+4\% = 5\%\).
questions.hint: Each variable's percentage error must first be multiplied by its own power before adding.
distractor_logic: Adds the two percentage errors directly (\(1\%+2\%=3\%\)) without first doubling velocity's contribution to account for its squared power.
Accounts for velocity's doubled contribution (\(2\times2\%=4\%\)) but forgets to add mass's separate 1% error at all.
Uses velocity's raw 2% error without doubling it for the squared power, effectively treating velocity as if it appeared to the first power, and ignores mass's error.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Using \(g=\dfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}\), if length l is measured with 1% error and time period T with 2% error, the percentage error in the calculated value of g is:
questions.explanation:
\(g\propto l^1T^{-2}\), so its relative error is \(1\times(\text{error in }l) + 2\times(\text{error in }T)\).

\(= (1\times1\%) + (2\times2\%) = 1\%+4\% = 5\%\).
questions.hint: T's error must be doubled before adding, since g depends on \(T^{-2}\).
distractor_logic: Adds the error in l directly to the error in T (\(1\%+2\%=3\%\)) without doubling T's contribution for its squared power in the denominator.
Doubles both l's and T's contributions instead of only T's, wrongly treating l as if it also appeared squared.
Accounts for T's doubled contribution (\(2\times2\%=4\%\)) but forgets to add l's separate 1% error at all.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: For a cube, mass is measured with 0.5% error and each side (used in \(V=\text{side}^3\)) with 1% error. The percentage error in the calculated density \(\rho=m/V\) is:
questions.explanation:
\(V=\text{side}^3\), so the relative error in V is \(3\times1\%=3\%\).

Since \(\rho=m/V\), relative errors add: \(0.5\%+3\% = 3.5\%\).
questions.hint: First triple the side's error to get volume's error, then add the mass's error.
distractor_logic: Adds the mass error to the side's error directly (\(0.5\%+1\%=1.5\%\)) without tripling the side's contribution to account for the cube power.
Accounts only for the volume's tripled error contribution, forgetting to add the separate 0.5% error from the mass measurement.
Reports only the mass measurement's error, ignoring the volume's error contribution entirely.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A quantity is calculated using \(Q=\dfrac{A^2}{B}\). If A has 3% error and B has 2% error, the percentage error in Q is:
questions.explanation:
\(Q\propto A^2B^{-1}\), so its relative error is \(2\times(\text{error in }A) + 1\times(\text{error in }B)\).

\(= (2\times3\%) + 2\% = 6\%+2\% = 8\%\).
questions.hint: Double A's error for its square, then add B's error as-is; never subtract in a quotient.
distractor_logic: Adds the two given percentage errors directly (\(3\%+2\%=5\%\)) without first doubling A's contribution for its squared power.
Subtracts B's error from A's doubled contribution (\(6\%-2\%=4\%\)), wrongly assuming errors can partially cancel in a quotient.
Accounts for A's doubled contribution alone (\(2\times3\%=6\%\)) but forgets to add B's separate error entirely.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: Two lengths are \(L_1=(10.0\pm0.1)\) cm and \(L_2=(4.0\pm0.2)\) cm. The difference \(L_1-L_2\), with its correctly propagated absolute error, is:
questions.explanation:
\(L_1-L_2 = 10.0-4.0 = 6.0\) cm.

For a difference, absolute errors always add: \(\Delta = 0.1+0.2 = 0.3\) cm, giving \((6.0\pm0.3)\) cm.
questions.hint: Subtracting the quantities never subtracts their errors — the errors still add.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two absolute errors (\(0.2-0.1\)) instead of adding them, wrongly assuming errors partially cancel when the underlying quantities are subtracted.
Reports only the larger of the two absolute errors, ignoring the smaller one's separate contribution.
Multiplies the two absolute errors together instead of adding them.

questions.topic: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A rectangular plate has length \(l=(5.0\pm0.1)\) cm and breadth \(b=(3.0\pm0.1)\) cm. The area, with its correctly propagated absolute error, is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Area \(= l\times b = 15.0\) cm\(^2\).

Relative error \(=\dfrac{0.1}{5.0}+\dfrac{0.1}{3.0} \approx 0.02+0.033=0.053\).

Absolute error \(\approx0.053\times15.0\approx0.8\) cm\(^2\), giving \((15.0\pm0.8)\) cm\(^2\).
questions.hint: For a product, add the relative errors of each dimension, then scale by the area.
distractor_logic: Adds the two absolute errors directly (\(0.1+0.1=0.2\)) as though this were a sum/difference case, instead of correctly combining relative errors for a product.
Computes the relative-error contribution from only one dimension and doubles it, instead of adding both dimensions' separate relative-error contributions.
Multiplies the two absolute errors together (\(0.1\times0.1=0.01\)) instead of properly combining relative errors and scaling by the area.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Add 125.67 cm, 8.2 cm, and 0.345 cm, reporting the sum to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Decimal places are 2 (125.67), 1 (8.2), and 3 (0.345); the least of these is 1 decimal place.

The raw sum \(125.67+8.2+0.345=134.215\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place, giving 134.2 cm.
questions.hint: Scan all three terms for the single one with the fewest decimal places.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, matching an intermediate term instead of the single most restrictive (fewest-decimal-place) term.
Reports the full raw sum with no rounding applied at all.
Rounds too aggressively, effectively treating the least precise term as having zero decimal places instead of the correct one.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Multiply 0.0234 by 1500 (written as \(1.500\times10^3\) to show 4 significant figures), reporting the product to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
0.0234 has 3 significant figures, while \(1.500\times10^3\) has 4; the least is 3 significant figures.

The raw product \(0.0234\times1500=35.1\) already has 3 significant figures, so it needs no further rounding.
questions.hint: Writing 1500 in scientific notation is what tells you exactly how many of its figures are significant.
distractor_logic: Reports 4 significant figures, matching the more precise factor instead of the less precise one.
Rounds too aggressively to only 2 significant figures.
Pads several extra unjustified significant figures onto the raw product.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Subtract 99.94 mL from 100.0 mL, reporting the result to the correct number of decimal places.
questions.explanation:
100.0 has 1 decimal place while 99.94 has 2; the least is 1 decimal place.

The raw difference \(100.0-99.94=0.06\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place; since the digit being dropped (6) is 5 or more, this rounds up to 0.1 mL.

Notice how subtracting two close numbers can dramatically reduce the number of significant figures in the result.
questions.hint: Subtracting two close values can leave far fewer meaningful digits than either original number had.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, matching the more precise term (99.94) instead of the less precise one (100.0).
Rounds 0.06 down instead of correctly rounding up to 0.1 at one decimal place.
Pads extra unjustified decimal places well beyond either term's actual precision.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Divide 0.00456 by 1.2 (both measured values), reporting the quotient to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
0.00456 has 3 significant figures, while 1.2 has 2; the least is 2 significant figures.

The raw quotient \(0.00456\div1.2=0.0038\) already has exactly 2 significant figures (3 and 8), so it needs no further rounding.
questions.hint: Leading zeros in 0.0038 are not significant; only the 3 and 8 count.
distractor_logic: Pads an extra unjustified significant figure (3 significant figures) instead of the correct 2.
Rounds too aggressively to only 1 significant figure.
Pads several extra unjustified significant figures, treating the division as though it were exact to many more places.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: A student computes \(12.5\times0.030\) and, separately, \(12.5+0.030\) (both measured, same units), each reported to the correct precision. Which pair of results is correct?
options: product \(=0.375\) (3 significant figures); sum \(=12.530\) (3 decimal places)
product \(=12.5\) (1 decimal place); sum \(=0.38\) (2 significant figures)
product \(= 0.38\) (2 significant figures); sum \(= 12.5\) (1 decimal place)
product \(=0.4\) (1 significant figure); sum \(=12.53\) (2 decimal places)
questions.explanation:
For the product: 12.5 has 3 significant figures, 0.030 has 2, so the raw product 0.375 rounds to 2 significant figures, giving 0.38.

For the sum: 12.5 has 1 decimal place, 0.030 has 3, so the raw sum 12.530 rounds to 1 decimal place, giving 12.5.
questions.hint: Apply the multiplication rule to the product and the addition rule to the sum — never swap them.
distractor_logic: Applies no rounding rule to either result, keeping the full raw values in both cases.
Swaps the two rules — applying the addition rule's logic to the multiplication result and the multiplication rule's logic to the addition result.
Rounds the product too aggressively and rounds the sum to the wrong, more precise number of decimal places.

questions.topic: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: In the number \(6.020\times10^{-3}\), how many significant figures does the number have?
options: only 6 and 2 are significant — 2 significant figures in total
only 6, 0, and 2 are significant — 3 significant figures in total
all digits plus the exponent's digit are significant — 5 significant figures in total
all four digits (6, 0, 2, 0) are significant — 4 significant figures in total
questions.explanation:
In scientific notation, every digit in the coefficient is significant, including zeros sandwiched between nonzero digits and trailing zeros after the decimal point.

The coefficient 6.020 has digits 6, 0, 2, 0 — all four significant. The exponent \(-3\) is never counted.
questions.hint: Sandwiched and trailing zeros in a coefficient are always significant; the exponent never is.
distractor_logic: Wrongly excludes both the sandwiched zero and the trailing zero, which are significant in a scientific-notation coefficient.
Correctly includes the sandwiched zero but still wrongly excludes the trailing zero.
Wrongly counts the exponent's digit (3) as contributing to the significant-figure count, which an exponent never does.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Assuming \(T=k\,l^a m^b g^c\) (k dimensionless) for a simple pendulum's time period T, in terms of length l, mass m, and gravity g, dimensional analysis gives:
questions.explanation:
Matching dimensions: \([T]=[l]^a[m]^b[g]^c\) gives \(M^0L^0T^1 = M^b L^{a+c}T^{-2c}\).

Comparing exponents: \(b=0\) (mass), \(-2c=1\Rightarrow c=-\tfrac12\) (time), and \(a+c=0\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12\) (length).
questions.hint: Match exponents of M, L, and T separately to get three simultaneous equations.
distractor_logic: Misapplies the exponent matching, doubling both the length and gravity exponents instead of correctly solving the simultaneous equations.
Wrongly assigns mass a nonzero exponent, even though matching the mass dimension on both sides forces \(b=0\).
Swaps the signs of a and c, inverting which quantity increases and which decreases the time period.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Assuming \(v=k\,P^a\rho^b\) (k dimensionless) for the speed of sound v in a gas, in terms of pressure P and density \(\rho\), dimensional analysis gives:
questions.explanation:
\([v]=[P]^a[\rho]^b\) gives \(L^1T^{-1} = M^{a+b}L^{-a-3b}T^{-2a}\).

Matching mass: \(a+b=0\). Matching time: \(-2a=-1\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12\), so \(b=-\tfrac12\). (Length checks out: \(-\tfrac12-3(-\tfrac12)=1\).)
questions.hint: Set up and solve the three exponent-matching equations for M, L, and T together.
distractor_logic: Misapplies the exponent matching, doubling both exponents instead of correctly solving the simultaneous equations.
Swaps the signs of a and b, inverting which quantity increases and which decreases the speed of sound.
Wrongly assigns pressure and density exponents the same sign, even though matching the mass dimension on both sides forces them to be opposite.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: A student claims dimensional analysis can derive the exact formula \(F=\frac12\rho A v^2 C_d\) (drag force), including the correct numerical value of the drag coefficient \(C_d\), purely from dimensional reasoning. This claim is:
options: true — since all the dimensional quantities in the formula are accounted for, the dimensionless factors follow automatically
true, but only when the formula involves exactly four physical quantities
false — dimensional analysis can confirm the equation is dimensionally consistent, but it can never determine dimensionless factors like \(\tfrac12\) or \(C_d\)
false — dimensional analysis cannot even confirm that this equation is dimensionally consistent
questions.explanation:
Dimensional analysis is a consistency check on the dimensions of both sides of an equation, not a way to compute pure numbers.

Quantities like \(\tfrac12\) and \(C_d\) are dimensionless, so they never appear in a dimensional check at all — their values must come from experiment or a more detailed physical theory.
questions.hint: Anything dimensionless is invisible to a dimensional check, by definition.
distractor_logic: Dimensionless factors carry no dimensions at all, so nothing in a dimensional check can ever reveal their numerical value.
The number of quantities in a formula has no bearing on this; dimensional analysis never determines a dimensionless constant, regardless of how many quantities are involved.
Dimensional analysis can indeed check this equation's consistency; what it genuinely cannot do is supply the dimensionless numerical factors.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of physical quantities have identical dimensional formulae?
questions.explanation:
Work \(=\) force \(\times\) distance, and torque \(=\) force \(\times\) perpendicular distance — both combinations give \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\).

Despite this, work and torque are physically distinct quantities (energy versus a rotational effect), which dimensional analysis alone cannot tell apart.
questions.hint: Both quantities are built from the same combination: force multiplied by a length.
distractor_logic: Impulse has dimensions \([M^1L^1T^{-1}]\) while power has dimensions \([M^1L^2T^{-3}]\); these are different.
Pressure has dimensions \([M^1L^{-1}T^{-2}]\) while force has dimensions \([M^1L^1T^{-2}]\); these are different.
Momentum has dimensions \([M^1L^1T^{-1}]\) while energy has dimensions \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\); these are different.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Work and torque share the same dimensional formula, \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\). What does this imply?
options: dimensional analysis alone cannot distinguish work and torque as physically distinct quantities — that distinction needs their different physical definitions, not just their dimensions
work and torque must always be numerically equal in any physical situation
the SI unit for torque should therefore always be written as the joule, just like work
one of the two quantities must have an error in its derivation, since they cannot share the same formula
questions.explanation:
Dimensional analysis only tracks how quantities combine dimensionally — it has no way of capturing conceptual differences, such as torque being related to rotation (a cross product) while work is related to a dot product along displacement.

This is a genuine, well-known limitation of the method, not a contradiction.
questions.hint: Matching dimensions is a necessary condition for equivalence, never a sufficient one for identity.
distractor_logic: Sharing a dimensional formula never implies numerical equality; it only means the two quantities are measured in dimensionally equivalent units.
By convention, torque is expressed in newton-metres rather than joules specifically to avoid confusing it with energy, even though the underlying dimensions are identical.
Two genuinely distinct physical quantities can perfectly well share the same dimensional formula; this is a known limitation of dimensional analysis, not an error.

questions.topic: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Checking \(v^2=u^2+2as\) dimensionally (v, u: velocity; a: acceleration; s: displacement), this equation is:
options: dimensionally inconsistent, since \(2as\) contains a numerical factor that \(v^2\) and \(u^2\) do not
dimensionally consistent, since \(v^2\), \(u^2\), and \(2as\) all reduce to \([M^0L^2T^{-2}]\)
dimensionally inconsistent, since a and s individually have different dimensions from v and u
impossible to check, since the equation involves squared quantities
questions.explanation:
\([v^2]=[u^2]=[L^2T^{-2}]\), and \([2as]=[a][s]=[L^1T^{-2}]\times[L^1]=[L^2T^{-2}]\) (the factor 2 being dimensionless).

All three terms match, so the equation is dimensionally consistent.
questions.hint: Combine \(a\) and \(s\)'s dimensions together and compare the result to \(v^2\) and \(u^2\).
distractor_logic: The numerical factor 2 is dimensionless and never affects a dimensional check; it does not disrupt the balance.

Individual quantities having different dimensions from each other is expected and irrelevant; what matters is that the combined term \(2as\) matches the dimensions of \(v^2\) and \(u^2\), which it does.
Dimensional analysis works perfectly well with squared quantities, as long as each term's overall dimensional formula is computed and compared consistently.

mixed_topics: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
questions.question: A screw gauge (pitch 1 mm, 50 circular divisions, no zero error) gives a main scale reading of 4 mm and a circular scale reading of 25 divisions. Express the measured diameter in metres.
questions.explanation:
Least count \(=\dfrac{1}{50}=0.02\) mm.

Diameter \(= 4+(25\times0.02) = 4.5\) mm.

Converting to metres: \(4.5\text{ mm} = 4.5\times10^{-3}\) m.
questions.hint: Compute the screw gauge reading first, then convert the final length into metres.
distractor_logic: Forgets to convert the millimetre reading into metres at all.
Uses a conversion factor of 100 instead of the correct 1000 between mm and m.
Introduces an extra unintended factor of 10 during the mm-to-m conversion.

mixed_topics: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: A rectangle's length and breadth are measured as \(l=(12.5\pm0.1)\) cm and \(b=(4.20\pm0.05)\) cm. Reporting the calculated area to the correct number of significant figures, the area should be written as:
questions.explanation:
12.5 has 3 significant figures and 4.20 has 3 significant figures, so the product needs 3 significant figures.

The raw product \(12.5\times4.20=52.5\) already carries exactly 3 significant figures, so no further rounding is needed.
questions.hint: Count each factor's significant figures separately before deciding the result's precision.
distractor_logic: Reports 4 significant figures instead of the correct 3.
Rounds too aggressively to only 2 significant figures.
Pads several extra unjustified significant figures onto the raw product.

mixed_topics: Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
questions.question: Surface tension has dimensional formula \([M^1L^0T^{-2}]\). Its SI unit, expressed fully in base units, is:
questions.explanation:
A dimensional formula translates directly into base SI units by substituting kg for M, m for L, and s for T.

\([M^1L^0T^{-2}]\) becomes \(\text{kg}^1\times\text{m}^0\times\text{s}^{-2} = \text{kg s}^{-2}\), since any quantity raised to the power zero contributes nothing.
questions.hint: A zero exponent on a dimension means that unit is simply absent from the final expression.
distractor_logic: Wrongly includes a length dimension, even though surface tension's dimensional formula has \(L^0\).
Invents a nonzero length exponent, even though the dimensional formula shows length raised to the power zero.
Drops one power of the inverse-time dimension, using \(T^{-1}\) instead of the correct \(T^{-2}\).

mixed_topics: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: A vernier caliper (least count 0.01 cm) reads 5.34 cm for one object, while a second object is read as only 5.3 cm due to a damaged vernier scale (readable only to the nearest main-scale division). Adding these two lengths and reporting to the correct number of decimal places gives:
questions.explanation:
5.34 cm has 2 decimal places, while 5.3 cm has only 1; the least is 1 decimal place.

The raw sum \(5.34+5.3=10.64\) must be rounded to 1 decimal place, giving 10.6 cm.
questions.hint: The damaged instrument's coarser reading limits how many decimal places the final sum can carry.
distractor_logic: Keeps 2 decimal places, matching the more precise reading instead of the less precise one.
Rounds too aggressively to zero decimal places.
Pads extra unjustified decimal places beyond what either reading actually supports.

mixed_topics: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: A student notes that \(F=ma\) is dimensionally consistent, and separately calculates the percentage error in a computed force as the sum of the percentage errors in m and a. Are both conclusions correct?
options: the dimensional check is correct, but the errors should be subtracted, since acceleration itself depends on other measured quantities
the error rule is correct, but the dimensional check is wrong, since force and mass cannot share the same base dimension
yes — \(F=ma\) is dimensionally consistent (\([M^1L^1T^{-2}]\) on both sides), and since \(F\propto m^1a^1\), percentage errors simply add
both statements are wrong — dimensional consistency has nothing to do with a formula's error-propagation rule
questions.explanation:
\(F=ma\) has dimensions \([M^1]\times[L^1T^{-2}]=[M^1L^1T^{-2}]\), matching force's known formula, so it is dimensionally consistent.

Since F is a simple product of m and a, their percentage errors add directly: \(\dfrac{\Delta F}{F}=\dfrac{\Delta m}{m}+\dfrac{\Delta a}{a}\).
questions.hint: A product's structure (like \(m^1a^1\)) directly determines how its percentage errors combine.
distractor_logic: How acceleration was originally derived is irrelevant here; once m and a are treated as the two measured inputs to F, their percentage errors simply add, never subtract.
Force's dimensional formula correctly includes mass as one of its base dimensions, \([M^1L^1T^{-2}]\); this claim is false.
Recognizing that F is a simple product \(m^1a^1\) is exactly what tells us to add the percentage errors; the two ideas are correctly connected here.

mixed_topics: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A time interval is measured as \(2.0\times10^{-3}\) s with an absolute error of \(2\times10^{-5}\) s. Expressed in milliseconds, this measurement is:
questions.explanation:
\(2.0\times10^{-3}\text{ s} = 2.0\) ms, and \(2\times10^{-5}\text{ s} = 0.02\) ms.

Both the value and its error must be converted by the same factor, giving \((2.0\pm0.02)\) ms.
questions.hint: Apply the exact same conversion factor to both the measured value and its error.
distractor_logic: Converts the error using a factor of 100 instead of the correct factor of 1000 for seconds to milliseconds.
Forgets that milli- already means \(10^{-3}\), effectively converting as though to micro-units instead.
Forgets to convert the absolute error at all, simply relabeling its original numerical value in the new unit.

mixed_topics: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: A student calculates g using \(g=4\pi^2 l/T^2\) from pendulum measurements, and separately checks this formula's dimensional consistency. Which statement is correct?
options: the formula is dimensionally consistent, and l should be measured with a metre scale or measuring tape rather than a vernier caliper, since pendulum lengths typically exceed a caliper's range
the formula is dimensionally inconsistent, since \(4\pi^2\) is a dimensionless factor that cannot appear in a valid physical equation
the formula is dimensionally consistent, but a screw gauge would be the better instrument for measuring l due to its higher precision
the formula cannot be checked dimensionally because it also involves a measurement technique for the length
questions.explanation:
\([g]=[M^0L^1T^{-2}]\) matches \([l/T^2]=[L^1]/[T^2]=[L^1T^{-2}]\) (the dimensionless \(4\pi^2\) does not affect this), so the formula is dimensionally consistent.

Since pendulum lengths are usually much larger than a caliper's or screw gauge's range, a metre scale or measuring tape is the practical choice for l.
questions.hint: Dimensional validity and practical instrument choice are two separate questions worth checking independently.
distractor_logic: A dimensionless factor like \(4\pi^2\) is completely permissible in a dimensionally valid equation; it simply does not affect the dimensional balance.
A screw gauge's very small range makes it entirely unsuitable for measuring a pendulum's length, typically tens of centimetres or more.
The technique used to measure l has no bearing on whether the formula itself is dimensionally consistent; these are separate considerations.

mixed_topics: Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: Five readings of a mass are 20.14 g, 20.12 g, 20.16 g, 20.13 g, and 20.15 g. Reporting the mean to a number of decimal places consistent with the readings themselves, the mean should be written as:
questions.explanation:
The mean of the five readings is \(\dfrac{20.14+20.12+20.16+20.13+20.15}{5} = 20.14\) g.

Since every individual reading was recorded to 2 decimal places, the mean is appropriately reported to the same 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The mean should match the decimal precision of the individual readings that produced it.
distractor_logic: Rounds to only 1 decimal place, discarding meaningful precision that the closely clustered readings actually support.
Reports an extra decimal place beyond what the original readings, each given to 2 decimal places, can justify.
Rounds far too aggressively, discarding essentially all of the measured precision.

mixed_topics: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
questions.question: A distance is measured as 3.20 km. Convert this to metres, stating the number of significant figures the converted value should carry.
questions.explanation:
3.20 km has 3 significant figures (3, 2, and the trailing zero).

Converting to metres by multiplying by \(10^3\) must preserve this: \(3.20\times10^3\) m, still 3 significant figures. Writing it as a plain 3200 m would make the significant-figure count ambiguous.
questions.hint: Unit conversion never changes how many significant figures a measurement carries.
distractor_logic: Writing the converted value as a plain integer without scientific notation falsely implies all four digits are significant, when only 3 are justified by the original measurement.
Drops a genuinely significant trailing zero from the original measurement, understating the actual precision.
Invents an extra digit of precision that was never present in the original 3.20 km measurement.

mixed_topics: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A vernier caliper (least count 0.01 cm) measures a rod's length in three trials: 8.40 cm, 8.43 cm, 8.46 cm. The mean absolute error of these readings is:
questions.explanation:
The mean of the three readings is \(\dfrac{8.40+8.43+8.46}{3}=8.43\) cm.

Deviations from the mean are 0.03, 0.00, and 0.03 cm; their sum is 0.06 cm, and dividing by 3 gives a mean absolute error of \(0.06/3=0.02\) cm.
questions.hint: Find the mean first, then average the magnitudes of each reading's deviation from it.
distractor_logic: Reports the sum of the absolute deviations instead of dividing by the number of trials.
Takes the single largest deviation as if it represented the mean absolute error, instead of averaging all three deviations.
Wrongly substitutes the instrument's least count in place of actually calculating the mean absolute error from the readings.

mixed_topics: SI Units: Fundamental and Derived Units, and Unit Conversion
Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: In \(E=mc^2\), if mass is expressed in grams and c (speed of light) in cm/s, the resulting energy would naturally come out in which unit, and how does it relate to the SI joule?
options: in ergs (the CGS unit of energy), where \(1\text{ J} = 10^7\) erg
directly in joules, since energy is always expressed in SI units regardless of the input units
in newtons, since \(E=mc^2\) fundamentally describes a force
the result would have no definable unit, since mixing gram and centimetre-based quantities is not permitted
questions.explanation:
Using CGS base units (grams, centimetres, seconds) throughout a formula naturally produces a result in the corresponding CGS unit — here, the erg.

Since \(1\text{ J}=10^7\) erg, the CGS and SI energy units are directly related, just at different scales.
questions.hint: The unit system of the inputs determines the unit system of the output, not a fixed SI default.
distractor_logic: The unit of a calculated quantity depends on the units actually used in the calculation; CGS inputs (g, cm/s) naturally produce the CGS energy unit, erg, not the joule.
\(E=mc^2\) computes energy, not force; grams and cm/s as inputs would never produce a unit of force regardless of the unit system used.
Using grams and centimetres together is entirely permitted within one consistent system (CGS) and simply yields the corresponding CGS energy unit, erg.

mixed_topics: Measurement Techniques: Length, Mass, Time, and Instrument Least Count
Accuracy, Precision, and Errors in Measurement
questions.question: A screw gauge's zero error is determined by averaging five separate zero readings: 0.02, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.04 mm, giving a mean zero error of 0.03 mm. Which statement about this determination is correct?
options: averaging is unnecessary, since zero error is fixed and a single reading would always give exactly the same result
averaging several zero readings is good practice, since it reduces the effect of small random variations and gives a more reliable zero error of 0.03 mm
the zero error should instead be taken as the largest reading (0.04 mm), to ensure the correction is never underestimated
since the readings vary, the screw gauge is defective and should not be used at all
questions.explanation:
Just like any other repeated measurement, zero-error readings can show small random scatter, so averaging several readings gives a more dependable estimate than trusting a single one.

Here the mean, \(\dfrac{0.02+0.04+0.03+0.02+0.04}{5}=0.03\) mm, is the value that should be used for the correction.
questions.hint: Zero error is measured the same careful way as any other quantity — by averaging repeated readings.
distractor_logic: Even a fixed systematic zero error can show slight variation between individual readings due to reading and placement effects, so averaging genuinely improves reliability.
Using the maximum reading rather than the mean introduces an unjustified bias, rather than reflecting the instrument's actual typical offset.
Small variation among repeated zero readings is normal and expected; it does not by itself indicate the instrument is defective.

mixed_topics: Significant Figures and Rules for Arithmetic Operations
Dimensional Analysis: Dimensional Formulae, Checking Equations, and Deriving Relations
questions.question: Using \(F=ma\), with mass 2.50 kg and acceleration 3.2 m/s\(^2\), calculate the force to the correct number of significant figures and give its dimensional formula.
questions.explanation:
2.50 kg has 3 significant figures and 3.2 m/s\(^2\) has 2, so the least is 2 significant figures.

The raw product \(2.50\times3.2=8.0\) already carries 2 significant figures. Since \(F=ma\), its dimensional formula is \([M^1]\times[L^1T^{-2}]=[M^1L^1T^{-2}]\).

questions.question: A digital stopwatch with least count 0.01 s records the time for 10 oscillations of a pendulum as 15.60 s. Express the period per oscillation in milliseconds.
questions.explanation:
Period \(=15.60/10=1.560\) s.

Converting to milliseconds (\(\times1000\)): \(1.560\times1000=1560\) ms.
questions.hint: Divide by the number of oscillations first, then convert seconds to milliseconds by multiplying by 1000.
distractor_logic: Misplaces a decimal point while converting seconds to milliseconds, off by a factor of ten.
Forgets to first divide the total time by the number of oscillations before converting to milliseconds.
Converts seconds to milliseconds using the wrong power of ten, dividing by 1000 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Using \(KE=\tfrac12mv^2\) (dimensionally \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\)), mass \(m=(2.00\pm0.02)\) kg and velocity \(v=(3.00\pm0.03)\) m/s. Find the percentage error in KE, and confirm the dimensional formula without using it to verify the factor \(\tfrac12\).
options: 3% error in KE; dimensional formula \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\), which only confirms the length-time relationship, not the factor \(\tfrac12\)
3% error in KE; dimensional formula \([M^1L^2T^{-2}]\), and this also confirms that the factor \(\tfrac12\) in the formula is correct
questions.explanation:
Percentage error in m \(=1\%\); in v \(=1\%\), doubled to 2% since v is squared. Total percentage error in KE \(=1\%+2\%=3\%\).

Since \(\tfrac12\) is dimensionless, \([M^1][L^1T^{-1}]^2=[M^1L^2T^{-2}]\); this confirms the equation's dimensional consistency but can never verify the numerical factor \(\tfrac12\) itself.
questions.hint: Double the velocity's percentage-error contribution because it appears squared, and remember dimensional analysis can never test dimensionless constants.
distractor_logic: Adds the mass and velocity percentage errors directly without doubling velocity's contribution for the squared term.
Correctly computes the percentage error but gives the dimensional formula of force instead of kinetic energy.
Wrongly claims that the dimensional formula's consistency can verify the dimensionless numerical factor \(\tfrac12\).

questions.question: A screw gauge (least count 0.001 cm, zero error \(+0.002\) cm) measures a ball bearing's diameter: main scale reading 0.5 cm, circular scale reading 25 divisions. Find the corrected diameter in metres, to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.explanation:
Observed reading \(=0.5+(25\times0.001)=0.525\) cm; since the zero error is \(+0.002\) cm, the corrected diameter \(=0.525-0.002=0.523\) cm.

Converting to metres: \(0.523\) cm \(=5.23\times10^{-3}\) m, keeping 3 significant figures to match the screw gauge's least count of 0.001 cm.
questions.hint: Subtract a positive zero error from the observed reading before converting units.
distractor_logic: Forgets to subtract the positive zero error from the observed reading.
Converts centimetres to metres with the wrong power of ten.
Correctly applies the zero-error correction but rounds to only 2 significant figures, losing precision the screw gauge's least count supports.
